opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a very exciting moment, because we have these machines that work remarkably well, and we don't really understand why. For a physicist, that's exactly the kind of situation you want to be in. There's a phenomenon, it's robust, it's reproducible, and it challenges what we thought we knew.

The central puzzle, to me, is the curse of dimensionality. If you think about learning a generic function in a very high-dimensional space, like images where you have hundreds of thousands of pixels, the number of examples you'd need grows exponentially with the dimension. It's hopeless. Yet these networks learn from a number of examples that is large but nowhere near astronomical. So the data must have a lot of structure, and the networks must be exploiting it. The question is: what is that structure, and how do the networks find it?

That question isn't only about machine learning. It's a question about the world, about images, language, and natural data in general. Why is a picture of a dog learnable? Probably because it's compositional: edges combine into textures, textures into parts, parts into objects. There's a hierarchy, and there's invariance. For instance, you can deform an image slightly and it keeps its meaning. In our group we've tried to make these ideas precise with simple generative models, such as hierarchical, grammar-like models of data, where you can actually compute how many samples you need and see how a deep network builds up a representation layer by layer. What's nice is that you can then go back to real data and test the predictions.

Diffusion models are another example. They let you probe the latent hierarchical structure of data directly. You add noise, go back, and look at which features change and which stay the same. You see something like a phase transition, where high-level class information suddenly flips while low-level details are recomposed. That gives you a new kind of experimental tool, almost a microscope on the statistical structure of data.

So I see AI as a stimulus in two directions. First, it's a new object to understand, like a new kind of physical system, with scaling laws, phase transitions, and collective behavior emerging from many simple units. Second, it's a lens that pushes us to ask sharper questions about the structure of natural data and maybe, eventually, about how learning works in the brain and in language. Ideally we'd end up with a theory that's not just a description of what these machines do, but tells us something about why the world is learnable at all.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI to a new physical system, but does not compare it with heat engines.

r002.rationale: It asks why networks learn and how they exploit data structure, but does not pose how AI generates novel outputs as a scientific problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that these machines put us in a position that physicists are actually quite used to, even if it feels new to people in computer science. We have an object in front of us that works extraordinarily well, and we don't really understand why. That's the situation physics was in with, say, superconductivity, or with turbulence, or with glasses, which is where I come from. You observe a phenomenon that is robust, reproducible, and surprising, and the surprise is the stimulus. It tells you your theory is missing something.

And deep learning is full of these surprises. The classical statistical learning picture says that if you have far more parameters than data, you should overfit, and yet you don't. In fact, performance tends to improve as you make the network bigger, which is the opposite of what the textbooks say. Then you have the fact that these models learn in extremely high dimensions, hundreds of thousands of dimensions for an image, and yet they avoid what we call the curse of dimensionality. If you took a naive view, the amount of data you'd need would be astronomical. So something about real-world data, and about the way these architectures interact with that data, is making the effective problem much lower-dimensional than it looks. Understanding what that something is, to me, is a genuine scientific question, not an engineering one.

What I find exciting is that we can now do experiments. In the past, if you wanted to study how structure in data can be learned, you were very limited, because learning was happening inside a brain and you couldn't probe it. Now you have a system that learns, that you can rerun with the same data and a different seed, that you can measure layer by layer. You can change the task, change the dimension, change the amount of data, and see how performance scales. Those scaling laws, the power laws people observe when they plot error against dataset size or model size, are the kind of thing a physicist gets very excited about, because an exponent is a signature. It constrains what the underlying mechanism can be. If I tell you the learning curve decays with a certain exponent, that should be derivable from some property of the data, perhaps its hierarchical or compositional structure, perhaps how smooth the function you're learning is along different directions.

So my view is that these machines are not just tools that happen to be useful. They are a new kind of physical system, in the sense that they exhibit emergent, collective behaviour that is not obvious from their microscopic rules. And they force us to ask what it means for data to be learnable at all, what the structure of natural data really is. I think that question, which is about the world as much as about the algorithm, is one of the most fundamental things we could be working on right now.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI with superconductivity, turbulence, and glasses, but does not compare it with heat engines.

r002.rationale: It asks how data can be learned and discusses emergent behavior, but does not pose AI’s generation of novel outputs as a problem for scientific explanation.

astra-6.text:
I think they provide a very interesting challenge for fundamental science, because we have systems that work remarkably well, but we don’t really understand why they work as well as they do. We know the rules by which we train them, but that’s different from understanding the behavior that emerges from those rules.

From a physics perspective, that’s quite a familiar situation. Knowing the interactions between particles doesn’t immediately tell you what a material will do. You need to find the right level of description, the quantities that matter, and perhaps some simplified models that capture the essential phenomena.

With learning, you can ask: Why does a large system generalize rather than simply memorize? How does the structure of the data affect what it learns? What determines how performance improves when you increase the amount of data or computation? These are scientific questions, beyond the engineering question of how to build a better machine.

And what makes this exciting is that you can do experiments. You can change the data, change the architecture, change the training procedure, and test an explanation. The challenge is to identify principles that explain something across many systems, rather than just describe one particular model.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI as a stimulus for scientific understanding but does not compare it with heat engines.

r002.rationale: It asks why systems generalize rather than memorize, but does not frame how AI generates novel outputs as a problem for scientific explanation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they provide a very exciting opportunity for science, because we have systems that work remarkably well, but for which we don't yet have a satisfactory theory. We know the rules by which they learn—we wrote those rules—and yet understanding what emerges from them is a very difficult problem.

That's a situation physicists are quite familiar with. Knowing the interactions between particles doesn't mean you immediately understand a liquid or a glass. You need to identify the relevant collective properties, and often you need simplified models that capture the phenomenon you want to explain.

For neural networks, one can ask: Why does increasing the size improve performance? What determines how much data is needed? How does the structure of the task affect what is learned? These are questions where I think statistical physics can contribute. But the ambition should be to make quantitative predictions that you can test, rather than simply to draw analogies.

And perhaps the most interesting possibility is that studying these machines will give us new concepts for understanding learning more generally. I wouldn't assume that an artificial neural network works like a brain. But it gives us a system in which we can control things and investigate which principles might be shared.

r001.rationale: The response compares neural networks to collective phenomena such as liquids and glasses, but does not compare AI with heat engines.

r002.rationale: It says understanding what emerges from AI systems is difficult, but does not clearly frame AI generating novel outputs as the scientific-explanation problem.
